Library Website - Problem Discovery and IA: The problem discovery phase included focus groups and interviews with every user group, including the Library departments, as well as web analytics and support ticket analysis. These conversations revealed fundamental IA and navigational issues where most language reflects Library internal structure which is not obvious for most users. A card sort with students confirmed they preferred shorter, noun phrase categories. 

 The IA was redesigned around user-facing language, with underexposed services repositioned into higher-visibility locations to close an awareness gap the research had surfaced. Tree testing is currently underway to validate the new structure.

The core problem wasn't visual: it was a misalignment between how the engineering team modeled the product and how winemakers actually think about their work. The platform was already live and being actively developed, which meant there was no opportunity to start over — only to course-correct in motion.

text: Winegrid - Feature Development: One of the more constrained design problems was the sensor scheduling interface. Users needed to set a daily reading frequency, subject to real technical limits: no more than once every 30 minutes, at equal intervals, with a configurable start time. Rather than expose those rules as form validation after the fact, the design enforced them through the affordance itself: a frequency slider constrained to valid values, paired with a visual scheduler showing all resulting readings, and a dynamically generated plain-language summary of the selection. The goal was zero-error input without requiring users to understand the underlying constraints. This was built and shipped in AngularJS.

text:
Banco de Tempo de Santa Maria da Feira - Problem: The Timebank of Santa Maria da Feira was a well-functioning community — validated membership, coordinator oversight, genuine participation — but it had a persistent imbalance: members offered services far more readily than they requested them. The assumption going in was that a cleaner digital interface would lower friction and increase exchanges. The actual problem turned out to be more fundamental. 
 Through field visits, informal conversations, and structured questionnaires, a different picture emerged. For most active members — many of them retirees — the primary motivation for participating wasn't economic. It was the sense of being valued and having company. One participant put it plainly: "If I need a ride somewhere, I don't request from the TimeBank, I take a cab." The barrier wasn't usability. It was how members framed their own participation, both internally and in how the network talked about itself. 
 This reframed the design challenge: the platform needed to make requesting feel like contributing, not consuming.

text:
Banco de Tempo de Santa Maria da Feira - Solution: Two prototypes were developed for different purposes. The first was built in WordPress — deliberately chosen because the platform would need to be maintained by coordinators without technical capacity. The goal was to test whether an off-the-shelf CMS could support the core workflows reliably before investing in a custom design. 
 The second was a high-fidelity prototype in Adobe XD, designed to validate the interaction model that came out of the research: a simple, familiar service-browsing interface that framed requests as participation rather than dependency. Usability testing with community members produced results that supported the hypothesis. One participant, who said they had never made a request before, responded: "Since it's this easy, I'll definitely start making some."
